summary: Specifies a host table format for ARPANET and Internet needs, covering host names and addresses plus network, gateway and operating system information. It replaced the format in RFC 608. Replaced by RFC 952.

plainLanguage.summary: Before there was a big online directory, every computer kept a list of names and addresses. This memo says how to write that list.

subtitle: Specifies the format for a central host table to map network names and addresses.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET and early Internet needed a way to maintain a central list of host names, network names, and gateway addresses, with information about what protocols and services each machine supported. The previous format in RFC 608 was no longer adequate.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a simple ASCII text format with one entry per line. Each entry specifies whether it is a network, gateway, or host, followed by its address, official name and nicknames, machine type, operating system, and supported protocols.
tldr.outcome: A machine-readable host table maintained by the DoD Network Information Center (NIC) that could be distributed to all connected systems. This was later replaced by the Domain Name System (DNS) in RFC 952.

facts.label: Address format
facts.value: Four decimal octets separated by periods

today: RFC 810 is from 1982 and is unknown status. It was superseded by RFC 952, which established the modern host file format, and later by the Domain Name System (DNS).

sections.title: The DoD Host Table
sections.content:
RFC 810 defines a standard format for a host table used across the ARPANET and early Internet. The host table is a central, machine-readable list of all known hosts, networks, gateways, and their associated addresses and capabilities.

The purpose is to provide name-to-address translation and information about what each machine is, what operating system it runs, and which protocols and services it supports. The table is maintained by the DoD Host Name Server at the SRI Network Information Center (NIC) and distributed to all participating systems. This specification replaces the format in RFC 608.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of it like a telephone directory: it lists computers by name, gives their address (like 10.0.0.73), and notes whether they handle FTP, TELNET, or other services.

sections.title: Host Table Entry Structure
sections.content:
Each entry in the host table is an ASCII text string with six fields separated by colons:

  • Field 1: Keyword indicating the entry type: NET, GATEWAY, or HOST
  • Field 2: Internet address (and optional alternate addresses)
  • Field 3: Official name and optional nicknames
  • Field 4: Machine type (optional)
  • Field 5: Operating system (optional)
  • Field 6: Protocol list (optional)

Fields 4, 5, and 6 are optional. Fields 3 through 6 apply only to the first address in Field 2. Each entry ends with a colon. NET entries cannot have alternate addresses or nicknames.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line in the list is like a note card: first you say what it is (HOST, NETWORK, or GATEWAY), then the computer's number, then its name, and optionally what operating system it runs and what services it has.

sections.title: Syntax and Data Format
sections.content:
The syntax uses specific delimiters and conventions. A semicolon begins a comment; anything after it on a line is ignored. Colons separate fields, with double colons indicating a null (empty) field. Commas separate elements within a field, such as multiple addresses or protocol specifications.

Protocol information is written as TRANSPORT/SERVICE (for example, TCP/TELNET or TCP/FTP). Some entries may specify only the transport (like TCP) or only a service name. Blanks (spaces and tabs) are allowed between elements but not within a single element. Continuation lines beginning with at least one blank character can split an entry across multiple lines.
sections.plainLanguage: The format is like a simple spreadsheet row: fields separated by colons, multiple items in one field separated by commas, and services written as type/name like TCP/FTP.

sections.title: Internet Addresses and Naming Rules
sections.content:
Internet addresses are 32-bit values represented as four decimal numbers separated by periods (for example, 10.0.0.73). Each number is one octet (0 to 255).

Names (for networks, gateways, and hosts) are text strings up to 24 characters using letters, digits, the minus sign, and the period. No blanks are allowed. The first character must be a letter, and the last must not be a minus sign or period. Gateways have -GATEWAY or -GW in their name; TIP or TAC machines have -TIP or -TAC. No distinction is made between uppercase and lowercase letters.
sections.plainLanguage: Every computer gets a number like 10.0.0.73 and a name like SRI-NIC. Names can have letters, numbers, and hyphens, but must start with a letter.

sections.title: Example Entries and Machine Information
sections.content:
The RFC includes example entries. A network entry looks like NET : 10.0.0.0 : ARPANET :. A gateway entry lists both addresses where it connects (for example, GATEWAY : 10.0.0.77, 18.8.0.4 : MIT-GW :: MOS : IP/GW :). A host entry might be HOST : 10.0.0.73 : SRI-NIC,NIC : FOONLY-F3 : TENEX : NCP/TELNET,NCP/FTP,TCP/TELNET,TCP/FTP :.

Machine types (Field 4) include names like PDP-11/70, DEC-1080, or CDC-6400. Operating systems (Field 5) include ITS, MULTICS, TOPS20, UNIX, TENEX, and others. The protocol list specifies both transport and service protocols available on that host.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry shows what the computer is, where to find it, its nickname, what kind of machine it is, what operating system it runs, and what services it offers.
